# Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering

Also called: Fourier window, Interpolation Methods, Interpolation Schemes for Frequency Domain Volume Rendering, Reconstruction Filters, Sample-and-hold, Zeroth-order interpolation

## Overview
Interpolation schemes for volume rendering reconstruct a continuous scalar field from discrete voxel data to evaluate density or opacity at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays. This family solves the problem of discretization artifacts (aliasing, blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling while balancing computational cost against spatial smoothness. It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like [Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution](1219-multi-sample-anti-aliasing-via-ray-distribution.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel itself rather than the statistical distribution of sample points, and from [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md) by operating in [voxel space](#3074-voxel-space.md) rather than depth space.

## Shared principles
All interpolation schemes in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in voxel space to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$ V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i $$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md)
[Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](#826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) is a [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) technique that performs resampling (zooming and shearing) in the frequency domain using [Fourier transforms](#2288-fourier-transform.md) to avoid blurring artifacts associated with spatial domain interpolation, particularly for large zoom factors. It exploits signal processing ideas such as the shifting theorem, the packing theorem, and the derivative theorem to achieve the best theoretical quality by using the ideal interpolation filter (sinc). Unlike standard spatial domain filters (e.g., B-spline, Catmull-Rom) or methods that zoom the intermediate image, this method resamples every volume slice in object space before projection, ensuring perfect reconstruction if the sampling meets Nyquist criteria.

### [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md)
[Fast tri-cubic interpolation](#848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) is a GPU-accelerated technique for reconstructing volume data using a cubic B-spline filter, designed to reduce the number of texture fetches required for the convolution sum. It solves the problem of high computational cost associated with evaluating the 64-term tri-cubic convolution sum by leveraging GPU linear filtering capabilities and separable kernel properties. It sets itself apart from standard [tri-cubic interpolation](#1077-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) by reducing the fetch count from 64 to 8 via pre-computed weight/offset lookups and multi-channel texture storage, and from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) by providing higher-order continuity and reduced aliasing at the cost of increased memory bandwidth for the lookup textures.

### [Bilinear Interpolation](858-bilinear-interpolation.md)
[Bilinear interpolation](#858-bilinear-interpolation.md) is a reconstruction scheme that estimates values at arbitrary 2D coordinates within a [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md) by performing linear interpolation first in one dimension and then in the other. It is primarily used in volume rendering for 2D texture sampling, triangle coloring in flat-shaded rendering, and as the foundational 2D component of [3D trilinear interpolation](#2613-3d-trilinear-interpolation.md). It differs from [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md) by operating only on the XY plane (or two dimensions), resulting in lower computational cost but requiring extension to the Z-axis for full 3D volume sampling.

### [Hardware Interpolation Approximation](1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md)
[Hardware Interpolation Approximation](#1027-hardware-interpolation-approximation.md) is a volume rendering technique that leverages graphics hardware rasterization to approximate the volume rendering integral. It solves the problem of efficient integration by assuming linear interpolation along ray segments, effectively mapping the volume data to polygonal primitives where the GPU's built-in interpolation performs the sampling. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on view-dependent, hardware-enforced piecewise interpolation (bilinear or trilinear) determined by polygon subdivision, rather than explicit, view-independent kernel-based reconstruction.

### [Trilinear Interpolation](1531-trilinear-interpolation.md)
Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value (e.g., density or opacity) at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values at the eight surrounding voxel corners. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts inherent in [nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md), which produces blocky, aliased images because rays rarely hit voxel centers exactly. It sets itself apart from [Frequency Domain Volume Rendering with Sinc Resampling](826-frequency-domain-volume-rendering-with-sinc-resampling.md) by using a compact spatial kernel (8 samples) rather than an infinite sinc function, and from [Fast tri-cubic interpolation](848-fast-tri-cubic-interpolation.md) by offering lower computational cost at the expense of reduced smoothness (C0 continuity vs C1).

### [Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation](2336-inverse-distance-weighted-interpolation.md)
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that generates a continuous 3D scalar field from discrete sample points by weighting nearby samples by the inverse of their distance raised to a power. It solves the problem of reconstructing a volume from irregular or sparse data (e.g., drill-hole assays) where grid-aligned interpolation schemes like trilinear are not directly applicable. While often applied to arbitrary point sets, specific implementations restrict the neighborhood to the eight vertices of the grid cell containing the query point. It does not guarantee $C^0$ continuity along interior faces of the grid.

### Variable Gaussian Blurring
Variable Gaussian Blurring is a reconstruction technique used to reduce visible artifacts from the discrete sampled nature of volume models, specifically false low frequencies caused by the Nyquist limit [S5, unofficial]. It involves applying variable Gaussian blurring to the source volume models before or during reconstruction to high-resolution 2D images [S5, unofficial]. The Nyquist Limit is defined as half the sampling rate, and infinite sampling of continuous surfaces is the only way to completely avoid artifacts [S5, unofficial].

### Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels
Barycentric Color Interpolation for Voxels interpolates vertex colors to a voxel center by treating the voxel center as a point inside the triangle and weighting the vertex colors by the areas of the sub-triangles formed with the voxel center [S6, unofficial]. The formula is $c = c_1 \cdot (A_2 / A) + c_2 \cdot (A_3 / A) + c_3 \cdot (A_1 / A)$, where $A_1 = \text{area}(v_1, v_2, P)$, $A_2 = \text{area}(v_2, v_3, P)$, $A_3 = \text{area}(v_3, v_1, P)$, $A = A_1 + A_2 + A_3$, and $P$ is the voxel center [S6, unofficial].

### Adaptive Interpolation for Isosurface Detection
[Adaptive Interpolation](#861-adaptive-filter-size-for-rendering-time-reduction.md) for Isosurface Detection interpolates input volume along rays at a predetermined sampling rate. It uses [non-binary classifiers](#6229-binary-and-soft-classification.md) to adjust the acceptable density range for an isovalue surface based on data change rate [S2, unofficial]. When data values change slowly, a narrow range of acceptable values is used for the isovalue surface; when data values change rapidly, a wide range is used to avoid missing the surface [S2, unofficial]. It supports user selection of interpolation: nearest-neighbor (preview), linear (day-to-day), cubic (publication-quality) [S2, unofficial].

### Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling
Interpolation Schemes for Projection-Slice Resampling are resampling filters applied to extracted projection-slices to control ghosting artifacts and rendering quality during Fourier volume rendering [S7]. Point-sampling (nearest-neighbour) filter clamps missing samples to the nearest available value, causing apparent ghosting artifacts when the volume is rotated [S7]. Trilinear interpolation filter reduces replica intensities and ghosting artifacts compared to point-sampling, with similar performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$ but higher cost for larger volumes [S7]. Hamming windowed-sinc interpolation filter with width 5 is a high-order reconstruction filter that maximally reduces ghosting artifacts when combined with zero-padding [S7]. Point-sampling and trilinear interpolation have nearly identical performance for slice sizes $\le 512^2$, but trilinear incurs higher performance overhead for larger volumes [S7].

## Background
The concept of interpolation in volume rendering originated with the need to handle the discrete nature of voxel data in ray-casting algorithms. Early work by Levoy [S2, unofficial] established the trade-offs between nearest-neighbor, linear, and cubic interpolation for ray-casting, noting that nearest-neighbor leads to blockiness and aliasing, while higher-order methods improve quality at increased computational cost. The use of [frequency domain methods](#1298-frequency-domain-based-method.md), specifically sinc resampling, was introduced by Westover [S4, unofficial] to address the limitations of spatial domain filters, particularly for large magnification factors. The development of GPU-accelerated techniques, such as fast tri-cubic interpolation [S1, unofficial] and hardware interpolation approximation [S1, unofficial], further refined these methods to leverage modern graphics hardware for real-time rendering.
